correctness.rationale: The exact circle exit transform and geometric successful-excursion conditioning yield the joint Laplace transforms. Dominated endpoint scaling proves the all-beta and asymmetric-side weak limits; Brownian hitting-time inversion gives the explicit joint density and Gamma marginals with universal correlation. A failed-segment Laplace transform gives joint independence from the total search clock. Coupling Brownian ring and half-line paths up to the opposite boundary, estimating the resulting sinh ratio, and accounting for an explicit incomplete-Gamma truncation term prove the stated finite-ring TV bound. The accompanying standard-library checker passed 219 deterministic finite checks; the infinity statements are proved analytically, not by testing.

originality.rationale: Closest published coverage was examined at statement/implication level: in particular the 2025 distributed-reset article already derives the general finite-rate last-reset-position law and Brownian first passage density, and the 2023 frequent-reset theorem covers the unmarked exponential limit. Neither of these prior results is presented as novel. The original claim assessed is the two-dimensional terminal-excursion marked scaling limit with its universal correlation, its independence from the total passage clock, and an explicit exponentially accurate finite-ring total-variation error for the pure-power family. None was located as an explicit or more general quantified theorem in the inspected primary sources or record searches. There remains a credible risk that this is implicit in general renewal transforms or a quantitative coupling theorem, requiring independent scrutiny.

value.rationale: In distributed stochastic search, the last starting site alone cannot determine how long the eventual successful travel segment takes. The new joint Gamma-mark law and parameter-independent correlation quantify precisely this coupling of location and duration, while an explicit exponentially small total-variation approximation supplies a mathematically controlled criterion for replacing a finite ring with a half-line at high reset rates. The density exponent also separates high-rate improvements from failures, giving a motivated model-design boundary. The contribution is a theorem about a natural observable pair and its geometry error, not a routine isolated moment or renaming of the known MFPT formula.
